Okay, I'm going to explain why this is wrong.

Let's present a hypothetical situation - you are going to get reeeeally drunk tonight. You know that you are going to get very drunk, you are planning on it. You will be out with your friend. Before you start drinking, you give your friend your keys, with the explicit instructions not to let you drive home.

This is a reasonable scenario, right? People do it all the time. They limit their future autonomy - essentially giving another version of themselves less autonomy than they would give themselves now. Why?

Or, to make an extreme point about parent-child relationships to establish a basic concept - a father should not give his three year old daughter the autonomy to decide when to walk out in the street, even if he would give that autonomy to himself. That is true, even if he views his daughter as an extension of himself. Why?

The answer to both is the same. If your parents are still responsible for you (and if they are good parents), they should want you to have autonomy in every situation when youare capable of understanding the situation and making well-reasoned decisions.

If you are a grown adult who owns your own life, your parents cannot stop you. If you are a minor, or are still living under your parent's roof, they have a responsibility to make sure that you are safe and are developing the ability to make good decisions before they hand you autonomy. Now, they may be doing that poorly and misjudging the amount of responsibility you can handle, but that doesn't mean they are obligated to treat you as they treat themselves, even if they view you as an extension of themselves.

If you don't like it, prove to them that you are capable of more. Or get a job, move out, and be responsible for yourself. Or stop crying.

It's not the same autonomy you have, it's the same autonomy you would give yourself. You know how boring it is to be stuck in someone else's paradigm, but you also know how incredibly dangerous and disorienting it is to be out of your element before you're ready. (Freshman year, first full-time job, kindergarten, junior high)
